llm.title: LLM server
llm.viaSshTitle: This engine's port is not reachable from the dashboard, so it is read through an SSH tunnel to the unit
llm.portHint: HTTP port of the LLM server on this Spark (vLLM / llama.cpp / sglang / ds4 / EXL3 / TensorFold / Radiance / OpenAI-compatible gateway).
llm.engineDecodeTitle: Live sliding-window decode rate. When that window is unavailable, the active-slot mean sums each active slot’s generated tokens divided by its elapsed time since first token; it excludes prefill time.
llm.perStreamTitle: Average decode throughput of one running stream (1 / mean seconds per output token). Only engines that publish a per-token latency histogram report it.
llm.notMeasuredTitle: The endpoint answered, but no rate could be measured on the last poll.
llm.prefillSglangTitle: Computed prefill tokens/sec over successive engine snapshots; cache-served tokens are not included. — means the counter baseline or a fresh snapshot is unavailable.
llm.prefillStrataTitle: Engine-reported mean for computed/new prompt tokens. It may be from an earlier prefill and is not an aggregate across slots.
llm.prefillDefaultTitle: Prompt tokens/sec taken in during the last poll window — cache-served + computed. Opening a saved chat in the UI does not hit the GPU; send (or regenerate) so the history is sent as the prompt. Cached prefill does little GPU work; uncached prefill is what builds KV cache.
llm.prefillingStrataTitle: A prompt is being processed; no current prefill rate is available.
llm.prefillingTitle: A prompt is being processed. The engine reports its speed only when the request finishes.
llm.perRequestTitle: Effective prefill rate of one request: prompt tokens ÷ prefill seconds over the finished window. The prompt counter includes prefix-cache tokens (this surface has no cached counter), so it is an effective speed, not raw GPU speed. The engine publishes prefill seconds only when a request finishes, so it is held between completions.
llm.perRequest: {{value}} tok/s per request — effective (incl. cached tokens)
llm.cachedPrefillTitle: Prefill tokens served from prefix cache (little GPU work). High values mean prompt reuse, not a faster cold prefill.
llm.uncachedPrefillTitle: Uncached (computed) prefill — tokens that actually build KV cache on the GPU.
llm.engineInfo: Active = processing or ready for requests. Sleeping = idle, GPU memory freed until next request.
llm.engineGeneratedTitle: Reported by the engine since it last started
llm.engineStateNaTitle: This backend does not report engine sleep state
llm.tipKvCache: SGLang reports the maximum pressure across full-attention and sliding-window pools. These pools have different denominators; free full-pool tokens are omitted when this pressure cannot describe them. Other engines show free tokens left in the engine’s KV-cache pool, over the allocated pool (tokens and memory). The pool is shared across concurrent requests and can be larger than one request’s max context. High usage (≥80% full) means little room for new or long contexts and often leads to queuing or preemptions.
llm.tipPhase: Recent engine snapshot activity. Prefill and decode rates use successive native counter deltas. Stale or unavailable snapshots are not reported as idle.
llm.tipBacklog: Estimated uncached prompt tokens awaiting prefill, including the current chunked prompt and queued requests. The engine estimates cache hits for requests not yet prefix-matched.
llm.tipRequests: Run / Wait are the engine's reported running and waiting queues. SGLang may keep a chunked prefill outside both queues: see Phase and Prefill backlog as well.
llm.tipTtftMean: Mean time-to-first-token reported by FreeToken (a mean, not a percentile): how long requests wait until the first output token.
llm.tipTtftP95: 95th percentile time-to-first-token from the engine’s request history: how long “slow” requests wait until the first output token. Spikes mean queueing, long prefills, or cold paths—not average decode speed.
llm.tipPreempts: Cumulative times the engine paused a running request to free KV cache for others. Rising under load signals memory pressure; zero is normal when the server is comfortable.
llm.tipPrefixCache: Lifetime fraction of prefix-cache lookups that hit (hits ÷ queries). Higher means more prompt reuse and less prefill work; — when the series is missing or unused.
llm.tipE2eP95: 95th percentile end-to-end request latency from the engine’s request history: arrival until the request finishes. Includes queue wait, prefill, and decode—not just token generation speed.
llm.tipItlP95: 95th percentile inter-token latency (time between successive output tokens) from the engine’s request history. Spikes mean decode stalls or contention; lower is smoother streaming.
llm.tipMtpAccept: Lifetime speculative / MTP acceptance rate (accepted draft tokens ÷ drafted tokens). Higher means speculative decoding is paying off; — when speculation is off or unused.

qa.measures: Basic accuracy on short, checkable questions: arithmetic, strings, dates. A quick sanity check that nothing is badly broken (a bad quantisation or KV-cache format shows up here first).
qa.how: 150 short questions: 30 fixed ones plus 120 generated from a fixed seed (multiplication, add/subtract, reversing a string, counting letters, sorting, binary, date offsets, least common multiple). The model answers directly, with thinking off.
qa.scoring: The reply has to commit to the answer, not just mention it. Numbers: the last number in the reply must be the answer ("1391" or "391 or 5" fail). Dates: the last date. Sorted lists: the last numbers, in order. Words and reversed strings: the answer as a whole word in a short reply, or a longer reply that ends on it. A reply that leads with the right number and then corrects itself, or hedges around the word ("not Canberra"), fails. A request error or timeout is not scored.
qa.settings: Thinking off · at least 64 tokens per answer · fast.

reason.measures: Multi-step reasoning: keeping several quantities straight through a story and doing the arithmetic in order.
reason.how: 40 word problems. Three people hold items, hand some over, one loses some, one doubles theirs, then everything is pooled and split into boxes. The question asks for two numbers: what is left over and what each box holds.
reason.scoring: The last line must be 'Answer: <left over>, <per box>' in the final answer (not the reasoning). Both numbers must be exactly right.
reason.example: Ana has 40 apples. Ben has 3 times as many as Ana. Cy has 12 … How many are in the jar, and how many in each box? End with 'Answer: <jar>, <per box>'.
reason.settings: Thinking on · up to 8192 tokens per answer · slower on thinking models.

arith.measures: Exact arithmetic over a long chain, where one slip anywhere makes the final number wrong.
arith.how: 40 chains: start from a 3-digit number and apply 10 operations in order (multiply, add, subtract, remainder then add 1000, divide rounding down). Every number stays a whole number.
arith.scoring: The last 'Answer: <number>' line must equal the true result (markdown and thousands commas are accepted).
arith.example: Start with 482. Then, in order: (1) multiply it by 7; (2) add 1530; … (10) divide it by 4, rounding down. What is the final number?
arith.settings: Thinking on · up to 12288 tokens per answer · slow.

track.measures: Keeping state straight over a long sequence of small changes, like tracking variables through a program.
track.how: 40 stories with five people who each start with some tokens, followed by 25 events: gives some to another, finds a few, or gives half (rounded down). The question is how many tokens one person has at the end.
track.scoring: The last 'Answer: <number>' line must be exactly right.
track.example: Track the tokens carefully. Mia starts with 34 tokens. … Mia gives 5 to Leo. Leo finds 3. … How many tokens does Leo have at the end?
track.settings: Thinking on · up to 12288 tokens per answer · slow.

gsm8k.measures: Grade-school maths word problems, the public GSM8K benchmark, so results can be read next to published numbers (as an approximation, see below).
gsm8k.how: 200 problems drawn once, with a fixed seed, from the GSM8K test set (MIT-licensed). The model solves each step by step and ends with its answer.
gsm8k.scoring: The last 'Answer: <number>' line (any capitalisation) must equal the dataset's final answer. $ signs, thousands commas, a % sign or a unit after the number ("18 dollars") are fine; a second value or a hedge is not.
gsm8k.example: A real GSM8K problem, e.g. a shop-and-change or distance-and-time story, followed by “Solve it step by step. End with 'Answer: <number>'.”
gsm8k.settings: Thinking on · up to 8192 tokens per answer. A sample of 200, not all 1,319, so a single score is only good to about ±4–7 points (95%); use the paired comparison for small differences, and do not compare with published GSM8K numbers.

mmlu.measures: Broad knowledge and exam-style reasoning across 57 subjects (law, medicine, maths, history, computer science and more), the public MMLU benchmark.
mmlu.how: 285 multiple-choice questions: 5 from each of the 57 subjects, drawn once with a fixed seed from the MMLU test set (MIT-licensed). Each shows four options A to D.
mmlu.scoring: The last 'Answer: <letter>' line (any capitalisation; text after the letter such as "B. Paris" is fine, "B or C" is not), or a reply that is just the letter, must match the correct option.
mmlu.example: The following is a multiple choice question about astronomy. … A. … B. … C. … D. … Reply with the letter of the correct answer.
mmlu.settings: Thinking off · up to 1,024 tokens per answer · quick. 285 questions, so a single score is only good to about ±5 points (95%); use the paired comparison for small differences, and do not compare with published few-shot MMLU numbers.

follow.measures: Following exact formatting instructions, the kind of thing that breaks pipelines that parse a model's output. Inspired by IFEval.
follow.how: 40 short writing tasks, each with 2 to 4 verifiable rules such as an exact number of bullet points, all lowercase or all capitals, a word count, required or forbidden words, no commas, a title in <<double brackets>>, or an exact closing phrase.
follow.scoring: Every rule is checked by code, not by another model. A task passes only when all of its rules are met.
follow.example: Write a short piece about how bees make honey. 1. Use exactly 4 bullet points, each starting with “* ”. 2. Do not use any commas.
follow.settings: Thinking off · up to 1024 tokens per answer · quick. Off by default so older overall scores stay comparable.

long.measures: Remembering and updating facts in a long document: whether the model finds the latest value, not a stale one, deep in a large context.
long.how: A long filler text with 16 “Remember this: the code for <animal> is <5 digits>” facts spread through it. Four of them are corrected near the end. The model is asked for the current code of every animal. You choose the context sizes (8k up to 256k) and how many items per size.
long.scoring: Passes when all 16 latest codes are right. A code that was corrected but answered with its old value counts as stale.
long.example: … Remember this: the code for otter is 48213. … Correction: the code for otter has changed, it is now 90471. … What is the current code for every animal?
long.settings: Thinking off · sequential, one at a time · can take many minutes at large sizes, and sizes that do not fit the model's context are skipped.
